units.title: Eager execution, autograd nodes and saved tensors
outcomes: Trace one eager operation from the Python call to its backward Function node and name each node on the path.
Explain which forward tensors autograd must keep for backward, how long they live, and what frees them.
Predict whether an in-place edit raises at the edit or at backward, and state what the version numbers mean.
units.why: Every memory number and profiler row later in this section is a consequence of this graph. If you cannot name the saved tensors, you cannot explain what checkpointing or the profiler is measuring.

next.note: Custom Functions build directly on save_for_backward and version rules.
Graph and saved-state reasoning locates stale-state and detachment faults.

study.title: How autograd encodes the history
study.locator: How autograd encodes the history: Function graph rebuilt each iteration, grad_fn entry points, what-you-run-is-what-you-differentiate

study.title: Saved tensors
study.locator: Saved tensors: the x-squared example, save_for_backward, _saved attribute inspection, the pow identity-True and exp identity-False examples with shared storage

study.title: In-place checks and saved-tensor hooks
study.locator: In-place operations with autograd and In-place correctness checks: version counters and the no-error-means-correct-gradients guarantee
study.depth: Skim Hooks for saved tensors after the pack_hook and unpack_hook contract. Skip the multithreading and complex-number sections.

focus: The graph is rebuilt from scratch every iteration. A grad_fn object from a previous iteration is stale and must never be reused.
Forward keeps only what backward needs. For x squared it keeps x; the rest of the forward temporaries are free to go.
Object identity of a saved tensor is an implementation detail. The pow case returns the same object and the exp case returns a different object, but both share storage and compare equal.
The first backward frees saved tensors. A second backward without retain_graph fails because the saved values are gone, not because the graph forgot the formula.
units.reproduce: Closed-book on CPU: build y = (x @ W + b).relu().sum() with small requires-grad tensors, walk y.grad_fn through next_functions, and write down SumBackward0, ReluBackward0, AddBackward0, MmBackward0 and AccumulateGrad in order. Then show (x ** 2).grad_fn._saved_self is x gives True while its storage is shared.
traps: Reading _saved_self is as identity proof. Packing may return a new object sharing storage, so test storage and equality, never identity.
Editing a leaf with requires_grad errors at the edit, but editing a saved non-leaf passes and fails at backward with a version error. The two messages describe different checks.
Assuming no-grad regions keep no state and therefore cost nothing. They keep no graph, but the forward compute and its live outputs still cost time and memory.

selfTest.q: For y = (x @ W + b).relu().sum(), name the backward node types from y down to the leaves.
selfTest.a: SumBackward0, ReluBackward0, AddBackward0, MmBackward0, then AccumulateGrad at each leaf.

selfTest.q: x.pow(2).grad_fn._saved_self is x is True, but x.exp().grad_fn._saved_result is y is False. Do both saved tensors share storage with the named tensor?
selfTest.a: Yes. Both compare equal and share storage. Whether packing returns the same object depends on whether the saved tensor is an output of its own grad_fn, which is an implementation detail.

selfTest.q: The first loss.backward() succeeds and the second raises about saved intermediate values. What was freed, and what flag keeps it?
selfTest.a: The saved tensors were freed after the first backward. Pass retain_graph=True to keep them for a second backward.

selfTest.q: Backward fails with expected version 0 but found version 1 on a saved tensor. What do the two numbers mean?
selfTest.a: The tensor was saved at version 0 and edited in place once since. Any current version above the saved version means gradients computed from it would be wrong.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: saved-tensor accounting and autograd-state instrumentation for the compact model.
units.stopWhen: You complete the reproduce walk without notes, and can predict for any small graph which tensors survive until backward and which edit raises where.

fit.note: The autograd mechanics note covers eager history, saved tensors and version checks at explain depth, with the mini-project supplying practice.

units.title: Streams, asynchronous copies and honest timing
outcomes: Explain why GPU launches return before the work finishes and where PyTorch syncs for you.
Order wait_stream and record_stream correctly when a side stream consumes a default-stream tensor.
Time a GPU operation with events and show why a bare wall clock understates it.
units.why: Every speedup claim in this section stands or falls on timing discipline. Async execution makes naive timers lie, and a hidden sync can pose as a slow kernel.

next.note: Apply event discipline inside annotated profiled phases.
Streams, overlap and sync cost return as first-class GPU topics.

study.title: Asynchronous execution and CUDA streams
study.locator: Asynchronous execution: enqueue semantics, CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING, and the Event timing example; CUDA streams: default-stream auto-sync, the wait_stream plus record_stream fix, and Stream semantics of backward passes
study.depth: Skip the TF32, GEMM precision, allocator-tuning and CUDA-graph sections here. They belong to later units.

study.title: Pinned memory and asynchronous copies
study.locator: Best practices, Use pinned memory buffers: pin_memory, non_blocking copies, and overlapping transfer with compute

study.title: Operations that force synchronization
study.locator: GPU specific optimizations, Avoid unnecessary CPU-GPU synchronization: the print, item, copy, nonzero and data-dependent-control-flow list

focus: Launches enqueue; they do not execute. On-device order is preserved per stream, and PyTorch syncs around CPU-GPU copies on the default stream only.
Side streams get no automatic safety. The consumer stream waits on the producer with wait_stream, and the tensor records its new stream with record_stream so its memory is not reused early.
non_blocking=True is a request, not a command. From pageable host memory the copy still syncs; pin the source first.
Backward follows forward stream placement. Grads produced under a side-stream backward must be consumed in the same stream context or after an explicit wait.
units.reproduce: On a CUDA GPU, time a 2048 by 2048 fp32 matmul both ways: CUDA events around the op with a synchronize before reading, versus a bare perf_counter around the launch. The event time lands in the tens of milliseconds while the bare clock shows a fraction of a millisecond, because it measures enqueue only. Exact numbers depend on hardware; the direction of the gap is the assertion.
traps: Timing with time.perf_counter and no sync, then reporting the result as kernel time. You timed the launch, not the work.
Calling .item(), printing a CUDA tensor, or branching on one inside the timed region. Each forces a sync and the stall gets billed to the wrong line.
Assuming default-stream safety extends to side streams. The docs sum example is wrong without wait_stream and record_stream even though nothing reads stale data.

selfTest.q: An Event-timed matmul reports 35 ms while a bare wall clock reports 0.2 ms. Which is the kernel time and why?
selfTest.a: The Event time. Launches are asynchronous, so the bare clock measures enqueue only. Events plus a synchronize measure the queued work.

selfTest.q: Data comes from pageable host memory with .to(device, non_blocking=True). Is the copy asynchronous?
selfTest.a: Effectively no. Asynchronous host-to-device copies need pinned source memory, so set pin_memory=True in the loader first.

selfTest.q: loss.backward() runs under torch.cuda.stream(s). Where may the .grad tensors be consumed?
selfTest.a: Inside the same stream context, or after the consuming stream waits on s. Using them on the default stream without a wait is unsafe in current PyTorch.

selfTest.q: Which of print(t), t.item() and t.to(cpu) force a host sync for a CUDA tensor t?
selfTest.a: All three. Each needs the values or the transfer finished on the host before Python continues.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: synchronized phase timing with explicit stream boundaries.
units.stopWhen: Your two-way timing shows the enqueue gap on your GPU, and you can point at the sync in any snippet that prints, copies, or branches on a CUDA tensor.

fit.note: The CUDA semantics note and the tuning guide cover streams, sync and timing at explain and measure depth, with the mini-project supplying practice.

units.title: GPU memory: allocated, reserved, peak and memory models
outcomes: Derive persistent training memory from parameter, gradient, optimizer-state and activation terms at stated precision.
Read allocated, reserved and peak counters and explain each discrepancy between them.
Separate live tensors, allocator reserve and outside-allocator memory when an OOM makes no sense.
units.why: OOM errors name a requested size but never the cause. The fix differs completely between live tensors, cached reserve and fragmentation, and only the counters tell them apart.

next.note: Trade the activation term for recompute once the model is measured.
Halve the parameter, gradient and activation terms with precision choice.

study.title: Mixed-Precision Training Memory Accountant
study.locator: Compute exact storage for parameters, gradients, saved activations, and optimizer state from tensor shapes and byte widths

focus: fp32 Adam training holds about 16 bytes per parameter before activations: 4 for the weight, 4 for the gradient, 8 for the two moment buffers. Precision and optimizer choice change the constants, not the method.
Allocated sums live tensors; reserved sums allocator segments. A 4 MiB tensor can sit inside 20 MiB of reserve, and nvidia-smi reports closer to reserve.
Peak counters are sticky. Reset them immediately before the measured region or the peak belongs to an earlier phase.
empty_cache returns unused segments to the driver. It never frees live tensors and never defragments them, so it cannot make a too-large tensor fit.
units.reproduce: Derive fp32 Adam memory for a 10M-parameter model as 160 MB before activations, then on a CUDA GPU allocate one 1024 by 1024 fp32 tensor and read memory_allocated as 4.00 MiB with memory_reserved strictly above it. State both numbers and which one nvidia-smi tracks.
traps: Reading nvidia-smi as live usage. It sees driver-side reserve, including cached segments and non-PyTorch allocations such as NCCL.
Calling empty_cache to fix an OOM and concluding memory is fine when it passes. The live set did not shrink; the next larger batch still fails.
Comparing a derived model against current allocated only. Peak across forward, backward and optimizer phases is the number that must fit, and it needs a reset counter.

selfTest.q: A 10M-parameter model trains in fp32 with Adam and no AMP. How many bytes do parameters, gradients and optimizer states hold?
selfTest.a: 40 MB, 40 MB and 80 MB: 160 MB total before activations, workspace, inputs and reserve.

selfTest.q: After allocating one 1024 by 1024 fp32 tensor, allocated reads 4.00 MiB and reserved reads 20.00 MiB. What is the extra 16 MiB?
selfTest.a: Cached allocator segments held for reuse, not live tensors. nvidia-smi tracks closer to reserved than to allocated.

selfTest.q: Peak grows every loop iteration while current stays flat. What was forgotten?
selfTest.a: reset_peak_memory_stats before the measured region. Max counters never decrease on their own.

selfTest.q: Will empty_cache let a run allocate one bigger tensor than the OOM size?
selfTest.a: No. It releases unused segments to the driver but keeps every live tensor, so a tensor that genuinely does not fit still fails.

units.title: Precision formats, autocast and gradient scaling
outcomes: Explain what TF32, fp16 and bf16 change about range, precision and accumulation, and state the current defaults.
Implement an autocast forward with a gradient scaler, including save and resume of scaler state.
Apply unscale before clipping with an unchanged threshold and diagnose skipped steps from the scale.
units.why: Mixed precision is the cheapest memory and speed win in training, but it moves range failures into the gradient stream where a wrong threshold or a stale flag silently changes the update.

next.note: Trace the overflow and underflow that scaling is designed to prevent.
Measure whether narrower math actually moved the bottleneck.

study.title: Automatic Mixed Precision recipe
study.locator: Adding torch.autocast with the fp16 linear output and fp32 loss asserts; Adding GradScaler with scale, backward, step and update; Inspecting/modifying gradients with unscale_ before clip_grad_norm_ at max_norm 0.1; Saving/Resuming with scaler state_dict

study.title: TF32 precision controls
study.locator: TensorFloat-32 on Ampere and later devices: the new fp32_precision settings per backend and operator, matmul versus cuDNN defaults, and the rule against mixing old and new APIs

study.title: Reduced-precision accumulation
study.locator: Reduced Precision Reduction for FP16 and BF16 GEMMs with the off switches; Reduced Precision Reduction for FP16 and BF16 in SDPA with the fp32 upcast default

focus: Autocast chooses per operation: matmul-like ops go narrow, reductions stay wide. A fp16 linear output with a fp32 loss is the contract working, not a bug.
The scaler exists because small fp16 gradients flush to zero. It scales the loss, unscales before the optimizer sees grads, and skips the step on inf or NaN.
Current defaults are full precision for CUDA matmul and TF32 allowed for cuDNN convolutions. Set them with fp32_precision, never by mixing allow_tf32 with the new API.
The recipe assumes a CUDA GPU. The CPU fallback is autocast with bf16 and no scaler, with its own dtype asserts.
units.reproduce: On a CUDA GPU, run a fp16 autocast forward over one linear layer and assert the output is fp16 while an mse loss over it is fp32. Construct torch.amp.GradScaler('cuda'), confirm the initial scale reads 65536.0, then run scale, backward, unscale_, clip_grad_norm_ and step plus update without error.
traps: Reading allow_tf32 after setting fp32_precision, or the reverse. Current PyTorch raises a mixing error, so pick one API and stay on it.
Clipping .grad between backward and scaler.step without unscale_ first. The threshold then applies to scaled values and silently clips the wrong updates.
Copying CUDA fp16 settings to CPU. The recipe requires a CUDA GPU; on CPU use bf16 autocast and do not expect the fp16 asserts to transfer.

selfTest.q: What are the current defaults for TF32 on CUDA matmul and cuDNN convolutions?
selfTest.a: Matmul uses full precision and cuDNN convolutions allow TF32. Both are set per backend or operator with fp32_precision.

selfTest.q: What raises when old allow_tf32 and new fp32_precision settings are mixed for one backend?
selfTest.a: A RuntimeError refusing the mix. The two APIs must not be combined.

selfTest.q: Scaled gradients sit in .grad. Where does clipping go, and does max_norm change?
selfTest.a: Call scaler.unscale_(optimizer) first, then clip with the same max_norm used in unscaled training.

selfTest.q: Why does fp16 training need a gradient scaler while bf16 training usually does not?
selfTest.a: Small fp16 gradients underflow to zero, so the scaler keeps them representable. bf16 keeps near-fp32 range, so plain updates survive.

practice.name: Learn PyTorch 10: mixed-precision timing rerun
practice.locator: Try mixed precision with larger model: uncomment the with and without mixed-precision epoch cells and rerun them
practice.note: Report your own per-iteration gap and explain it with the profiler's Tensor Core share, as the chapter does with its 9 to 12 percent reading.

units.stopWhen: Your autocast plus scaler loop asserts the right dtypes, clips at an unchanged threshold, and you can explain any skipped step from the scale history.

fit.note: The AMP recipe plus the TF32 and reduced-precision notes cover formats, scaler order and defaults, with the notebook rerun giving practice.

units.title: Overflow, underflow and finding the first invalid value
outcomes: Explain why mathematically identical floating-point computations may differ bitwise across batches, slices and backends.
Enable anomaly detection to name the first backward function that produces NaN, with its forward traceback.
Place isfinite checks so an invalid value is caught at creation, not ten steps later.
units.why: A NaN loss names no culprit. The only cheap evidence is the first invalid value and the operation that made it, and both need instrumentation in place before the failure.

next.note: Promote first-invalid evidence into full divergence diagnosis.
Record invalid events alongside phase timings in profiles.

study.title: Nonassociativity, batches, slices and extremal values
study.locator: Opening paragraphs on limited accuracy and nonassociativity; Batched computations or slice computations with the bmm and sum examples; Extremal values with the norm overflow example and the isfinite advice

study.title: Anomaly detection reference
study.locator: detect_anomaly and set_detect_anomaly: forward traceback of the failing operation plus the check_nan error on NaN generated in backward; debug-only slowdown warning

study.title: Debugging APIs stay off in timed runs
study.locator: General optimizations, Disable debugging APIs: anomaly detection, profiler hooks and gradcheck off for regular training

focus: Floating point addition and multiplication are not associative. Batching, slicing and backend choice change reduction order, so bitwise identity is never promised.
Overflow can strike intermediates while the final value is representable. The fp32 norm of [1e20, 1e20] is inf while the fp64 norm is finite.
Anomaly detection answers which backward made NaN, not which forward looked odd. check_nan fires on NaN generated inside backward.
Detection and profiling both slow execution. Neither belongs in a timed run or a production loop.
units.reproduce: On CPU, show torch.tensor([1e20, 1e20]).norm() gives inf while the double version is finite. Then run (x / x).backward() at x = 0 under autograd.detect_anomaly() and record the exact error naming DivBackward0 and its NaN output.
traps: Asserting bitwise equality across batch sizes, slices or devices. The docs promise nothing here; compare with a tolerance.
Expecting anomaly detection to flag NaN flowing from forward. Log of a negative is NaN forward with a finite grad of -1, and check_nan stays silent because backward generated nothing invalid.
Leaving anomaly detection or the profiler on while timing. Both add overhead, so a slow profiled run proves nothing about the clean run.

selfTest.q: Under detect_anomaly, (x / x).backward() at x = 0 names DivBackward0. What does that name identify?
selfTest.a: The backward function whose output went NaN, hence the forward division. The mode also prints the traceback of that forward call.

selfTest.q: torch.log of -1.0 gives NaN forward and grad -1.0 with no anomaly error. Why silent?
selfTest.a: check_nan fires on NaN generated by backward computation. Here backward computed the finite value 1/x, so there is nothing to report.

selfTest.q: (A@B)[0] equaled A[0]@B[0] bitwise on your machine. May a test assert == across batchings?
selfTest.a: No. Bitwise identity across batched and unbatched paths is not guaranteed, so assert allclose with an explicit tolerance.

selfTest.q: Times look bad with anomaly detection and the profiler enabled. What is the first correction?
selfTest.a: Disable both for timed runs. Both are debug-only overhead, so their timings do not describe the clean run.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: first-invalid capture and seeded NaN diagnosis with fixed-batch replay.
units.stopWhen: You can produce the named DivBackward0 error on demand, and every equality in your checks carries an explicit tolerance.

fit.note: The numerical accuracy note and the anomaly reference cover nonassociativity, overflow and first-invalid tooling, with the mini-project supplying practice.

units.title: Activation checkpointing and recomputation
outcomes: Wrap a segment with torch.utils.checkpoint and state exactly what stays alive and what is recomputed.
Choose use_reentrant False with reasons, and pass it explicitly.
Measure the memory saving against the recompute cost and the RNG effects.
units.why: Checkpointing converts the activation term of the memory model into extra compute. Done blindly it slows training for no reason; done deliberately it is what lets larger batches fit.

next.note: Attribute the recompute cost to the backward phase in a profile.
Recomputation policy scales with sharded and pipeline-parallel training later.

study.title: torch.utils.checkpoint API
study.locator: checkpoint signature and semantics: only args stay alive, region outputs are recomputed in backward; use_reentrant False versus True differences; preserve_rng_state with the multi-device caveat; determinism_check and debug

study.title: Which layers to checkpoint
study.locator: General optimizations, Checkpoint intermediate buffers: large layer outputs with small recompute cost as targets

focus: Only the checkpoint inputs stay alive; everything the region computes is rerun in backward. Memory saved equals the dropped forward tensors minus the inputs.
Non-reentrant is the recommended path: it supports grad, keyword args and nested structures, and it stops recomputation early once the needed activations exist.
RNG state is stashed and restored by default so dropout masks match. Turning that off changes gradients, not forward outputs.
Recompute reruns the region code. Globals read inside the region, device moves, and multi-device RNG all break the equivalence silently or loudly.
units.reproduce: On CPU, checkpoint a dropout block with use_reentrant=False and show its gradients are bitwise equal to the plain block at the same seed. Rerun with preserve_rng_state=False and show the gradients differ while the forward outputs still match.
traps: Omitting use_reentrant and assuming a default. Current PyTorch warns that it must be passed explicitly; pass False deliberately.
Wrapping tiny cheap regions. Recompute then costs more than the memory it saves; target large outputs with small recompute cost.
Changing code or globals between forward and backward. The recompute must see the identical function, or gradients are silently wrong.

selfTest.q: What stays alive across a checkpointed region, and what is recomputed?
selfTest.a: Only the input args stay alive. The region reruns in backward to rebuild every forward tensor it needs.

selfTest.q: With preserve_rng_state False, forward outputs still match but gradients differ. Why?
selfTest.a: Forward runs once either way. The flag only controls the RNG state used by the backward recompute, so only dropout-dependent gradients change.

selfTest.q: What happens when use_reentrant is omitted, and which value is recommended?
selfTest.a: PyTorch warns that it must be passed explicitly. False is recommended: it supports grad, kwargs and nested structures with early stop.

selfTest.q: Why does the reentrant variant refuse detached tensors and inputs without requires_grad?
selfTest.a: It runs forward under no_grad with no recorded graph, so there is nothing to differentiate and gradients come back None.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: activation-checkpointing memory savings with equivalence checks.
units.stopWhen: Your checkpointed block matches plain gradients bitwise at fixed seed, and you can price any block in memory saved versus recompute added.

fit.note: The checkpoint reference covers semantics, variant differences and RNG behavior, with the mini-project supplying practice.

units.title: Complete checkpoints, atomic writes and reproducibility boundaries
outcomes: Save and restore every state a resume needs: model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, epoch, RNG and data position.
Write checkpoints atomically so a crash never leaves a half-written file on the load path.
State the exact reproducibility boundary: what matches bitwise, what matches statistically, and what never matches.
units.why: Resume bugs waste entire training runs: the loss looks fine while the data order, the schedule, or the augmentation stream quietly diverges. The checkpoint contract is what makes a restart a continuation instead of a new experiment.

next.note: Use resume equivalence as a control when a restarted run diverges.
Complete state grows into sharded and multi-worker resume later.

study.title: General checkpoints for resume
study.locator: What is a state_dict; Saving and Loading a General Checkpoint: save and load patterns, optimizer state, 2 to 3 times model size, .tar convention, eval versus train mode; the best_model_state reference pitfall
study.depth: Skip Saving an Exported Program and the DataParallel section unless your model uses them.

study.title: Reproducibility: seeds, determinism and data loading
study.locator: Controlling sources of randomness including manual_seed across devices; Avoiding nondeterministic algorithms with the cross-release and CPU-versus-GPU limits; DataLoader worker seeding with worker_init_fn and generator; CUDA convolution benchmarking versus determinism

study.title: Atomic renames for checkpoint writes
study.locator: os.replace: a successful rename is atomic, so write the checkpoint to a temp file in the same directory, flush and fsync, then replace the final name

focus: A resume checkpoint is a dict of state, not a model file: epoch, model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, RNG states and the sampler position all belong in it.
state_dict returns references to live tensors. Training on after building the dict mutates the saved copy too; serialize to disk or deepcopy at save time.
Per-worker RNG needs explicit construction. A Generator built in Dataset init is fork-copied identically into every worker and repeats its stream.
Bitwise resume holds on one machine, one build, one device kind. Across releases, platforms, or CPU versus GPU, only statistical equivalence is promised.
units.reproduce: On CPU, train 3 steps, save the full dict to disk, train 2 more, then load the disk file into fresh model and optimizer objects, restore the RNG state, run 2 steps, and show bitwise equal weights. Rerun the resume without restoring RNG and show it diverges.
traps: Reloading from the in-memory dict after further training. The dict aliases live optimizer buffers, so the resume silently starts from the later state.
Seeding only torch.manual_seed with several DataLoader workers. Global RNGs get per-worker seeds, but a copied Generator object repeats exactly; build it per worker from torch.initial_seed.
Writing the checkpoint straight to the final name. A mid-write crash leaves a corrupt file on the load path; temp file plus os.replace avoids it.

selfTest.q: Name the minimum checkpoint contents for exact CPU resume of SGD with momentum, a StepLR scheduler, AMP and a shuffled loader.
selfTest.a: Model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, epoch, torch and CUDA RNG states, and the sampler position or loader generator state.

selfTest.q: A saved dict is kept in memory, training continues, then a fresh optimizer loads that dict. Why are its buffers wrong?
selfTest.a: state_dict returns references, so continued training mutated the same buffers the dict aliases. Serialize to disk or deepcopy at save time.

selfTest.q: Two DataLoader workers emit identical augmentation streams. State the bug and the fix.
selfTest.a: A Generator built in Dataset init was fork-copied identically into both workers. Build it per worker from torch.initial_seed in worker_init_fn, or pass a generator.

selfTest.q: The job dies mid-write and the checkpoint is corrupt. What write pattern survives this?
selfTest.a: Write to a temp file in the same directory, flush and fsync, then os.replace onto the final name. Readers only ever see complete files.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: resume equivalence and interruption handling with declared tolerances.
units.stopWhen: Your disk-roundtrip resume matches the continuous run bitwise, and a changed-seed or unrestored-RNG resume is caught by your own equivalence check.

fit.note: Coverage failed for atomic checkpoint writes; Python's os.replace reference fills that gap beside the PyTorch save and reproducibility docs.

units.title: torch.compile: capture, guards, graph breaks and dynamic shapes
outcomes: Compile a stable fragment and prove eager equivalence on values and gradients.
Trigger a graph break and a recompilation on purpose, then read each from the logs.
Choose fullgraph, dynamic and backend settings from the failure you want to forbid or allow.
units.why: Compile silently accepts partial graphs: a break just runs that part eagerly. Without break counts and equivalence checks, a speedup number can hide a semantics change.

next.note: Measure compiled versus eager inside profiled phases.
Capture, guards and backends return at deployment time.

study.title: torch.compile parameters
study.locator: fullgraph, dynamic, backend and mode; guard failures with TORCH_LOGS=guards; recompile_limit of 8 before falling back to eager

study.title: Breaks, guards, recompiles and logs
study.locator: Terminology with the graph break, guards, recompilation and dynamic shapes definitions; Logging Tools with TORCH_LOGS graph_breaks, guards and recompiles; Simple Workarounds including data-dependent fixes; Reporting Issues, Ablation with eager and inductor backends
study.depth: Read Terminology, Logging Tools and Simple Workarounds fully. Skim TorchDynamo internals and Reporting Issues.

focus: Default compile is partial: each frame compiles what it can and runs the rest eagerly. fullgraph=True turns an unnoticed break into a loud error.
Guards are runtime checks on shapes, types and values. A failed guard recompiles, and eight recompiles exhaust the budget and fall back to eager.
Data-dependent control flow is the classic break: .item, tensor conditions and prints split the graph. Hoist, use torch.cond, or capture scalar outputs.
Equivalence comes before timing. Compare eager and compiled values and gradients with a tolerance, across shapes, before believing any speedup.
units.reproduce: Compile a pure function and assert eager and compiled outputs match. Then compile a branch on flag.item(): read the log line naming Tensor.item() as the break, show fullgraph=True raises on it, and show dynamic=False compiling one graph per shape with a counter of unique graphs.
traps: Reporting a speedup without a break count. A fully broken compile is just eager with overhead, and the timer will not tell you.
Closing over Python floats or scheduler values. Guards treat them as constants and recompile per value; wrap them in tensors.
Assuming dynamic shapes are free. Dynamic kernels avoid recompiles only where ops allow; overspecialization still needs the dynamic log to diagnose.

selfTest.q: Compiled code matches eager but the log names Tensor.item() as a graph break. What happened to the function?
selfTest.a: Dynamo split it at the .item() call and runs that part eagerly. Fix by hoisting the value out, using torch.cond, or enabling scalar capture.

selfTest.q: Under dynamic=False, one shape reuses its graph while a new shape adds a second. What does dynamic=True change?
selfTest.a: It traces shape-generic kernels up front to avoid one recompile per shape, where the operations allow it.

selfTest.q: Timing collapses to eager speed after several shape changes. Which limit fired, and how do you see why?
selfTest.a: The recompile limit, default 8, fell back to eager. Inspect the failing guards with TORCH_LOGS=recompiles.

selfTest.q: Why compare values and gradients with tolerance before trusting a compile speedup?
selfTest.a: Partial capture or specialization can change numerics. Equivalence first proves the speedup measures the same computation.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: triggered graph-break repair with eager comparison.
units.stopWhen: You can trigger, name and fix one break and one recompile from the logs, with eager equivalence holding across your test shapes.

fit.note: The compile reference and the troubleshooting guide cover capture, guards, breaks and dynamic shapes at measure depth, with the mini-project supplying practice.

units.title: Profiling training phases and verifying optimizations
outcomes: Annotate a training step and attribute time to data wait, transfer, forward, backward and optimizer phases.
Read self versus total time and memory, and split shared operators by input shape.
Revalidate learning and resume behavior after any optimization, and explain one model-versus-measured discrepancy.
units.why: Optimization without a phase breakdown optimizes the wrong line. The profile decides whether the step is data-starved, launch-bound, compute-bound or sync-bound, and the revalidation proves the faster run still learns.

next.note: Reuse the overfit and shuffled-label controls as learning checks.
Phase analysis generalizes to kernels, overlap and roofline work.

study.title: Transformer Training FLOP Estimator
study.locator: Estimate one training step from forward matrix multiplications and a supplied forward attention cost

focus: Annotate before measuring: one range per phase with record_function, plus DataLoader timing outside the step, so data wait cannot hide inside forward.
Self time excludes children and total includes them. A big total with small self points at the children, not at the named line.
Predict first, then profile. Write the expected slowest phase and the expected memory peak before running, and explain the residual in writing.
Every optimization revalidates learning: loss, gradients, controls and resume. A faster run that learns differently is a defect, not a win.
units.reproduce: On CPU, profile one annotated step of a small MLP with forward, backward and optimizer ranges. Show the train_step total covers its children, export the chrome trace to a nonempty file, and write one sentence attributing the largest phase.
traps: Profiling with stacks, anomaly detection or gradcheck on and calling it a measurement. Debug tooling distorts the run; measure the clean configuration.
Tuning the fastest phase. Rank phases first; a 2x win on 5 percent of the step is noise against an unexamined data wait.
Skipping learning checks after AMP, compile or fusion. Numerics move silently; rerun controls and resume checks before keeping the change.

selfTest.q: key_averages shows forward total 55 percent but self 13 percent. Where is the rest?
selfTest.a: In child operators such as addmm. Self excludes children while total includes them.

selfTest.q: One aten operator appears twice with different shapes. Which flags produce that split?
selfTest.a: record_shapes True with group_by_input_shape True on the averages.

selfTest.q: The memory table shows aten::empty with large self memory and convolutions with none. What does that mean?
selfTest.a: empty performs the allocation, so it owns the self bytes. The convolutions allocate through calls beneath them.

selfTest.q: After AMP, compile and a larger batch, loss matches but step time barely moves. Name the next two checks.
selfTest.a: Read which phase dominates; the bottleneck may be data wait or sync, not math. Then confirm debug tooling is off before further tuning.
